P0A8F.description: P0A8F means the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter for the 12 V network) does not perform as expected even though its signals are electrically in range. GM's 2013 eAssist tables use it as a correlation test: with the APM commanded on and ignition voltage 9 to 32 V, the APM's own low-voltage reading and the run/crank voltage measured by the controller must agree within 4.5 V. A larger difference over 3.75 s in a 5 s window sets the code as Type B, two trips to MIL. A high resistance in the 12 V output path or ground, a drifting sensor or a converter that cannot hold its target can all cause this. P0A8D and P0A8E cover sensor circuit low/high faults.

causes.label: High resistance in 12 V output cable, fuse link or ground
Drifting voltage sensor in the module
Converter unable to hold its target voltage

symptoms: MIL and charging/hybrid warning
Low or fluctuating 12 V voltage

P0A90.title: Drive Motor A Performance
P0A90.description: P0A90 reports that electric drive motor A does not behave as commanded. In GM's eAssist mild hybrid the motor/generator is belt-driven from the crankshaft, so GM uses P0A90 to detect a slipping or broken belt: the motor speed is compared with the engine speed. In 2013 a difference above 1000 rpm for 1.5 s, or repeated smaller slips above 500 rpm on two key cycles, set it; the 2016 tables use more than 1500 rpm for about 5.6 s or repeated 1000 rpm slip events. GM rates it Type A, MIL on the first trip. In full hybrids the generic definition applies to speed or torque deviations of the traction motor. P0A91 is the equivalent for motor B, P0A92 for the generator.

causes.label: Slipping, worn or broken drive belt on belt-driven motor/generators
Faulty belt tensioner or contamination on the belt
Motor, position sensor or inverter fault in full hybrids

symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning
Belt squeal or auto-stop/start not working
Reduced electric assist or limp mode

P0A91.title: Drive Motor B Performance
P0A91.description: P0A91 is set when the second electric drive motor (motor B) of a hybrid or electric vehicle does not deliver the expected speed or torque, although no electrical circuit fault is detected. Motor B exists only on systems with two traction motors, such as power-split or dual-motor layouts. CARB requires hybrid OBD systems to monitor electric motor performance. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's tables describe the motor A equivalent P0A90 as a comparison between motor speed and a reference speed, which illustrates the approach. Causes range from inverter or resolver faults to mechanical damage. The vehicle usually limits power or enters a reduced mode. P0A79 covers inverter B performance.

causes.label: Inverter B fault limiting motor current
Motor position sensor (resolver) signal error
Mechanical damage to motor B or its gearing

symptoms: Hybrid/EV system warning and MIL
Reduced power or limp mode

P0A92.title: Hybrid Generator Performance
P0A92.description: P0A92 indicates that the generator of a hybrid system, the electric machine mainly used to convert engine power into electrical energy, does not reach the expected output, speed or torque. CARB requires manufacturers to describe how they monitor the generator so that faults preventing it from working are detected. FCA documents the code for the 2020 Jeep Compass and Renegade plug-in hybrids (bulletin 08-057-21): it appears together with drive motor phase current sensor codes, and the fix is a software update of the hybrid control processor and power inverter module. A turtle (limp home) lamp may accompany it. P0A90/P0A91 cover the drive motors; P0A3F and similar codes cover generator position sensing.

causes.label: Hybrid controller or inverter software needing update (documented by FCA)
Inverter phase current sensing fault
Internal generator fault (winding, bearing, position sensor)

symptoms: MIL and hybrid system warning
Limp home (turtle) lamp, reduced power
Reduced charging of the high-voltage battery

P0A93.title: Inverter A Cooling System Performance
P0A93.description: The power inverter of a hybrid has its own coolant circuit with an electric pump, radiator and fan, separate from engine cooling. P0A93 is set when this circuit does not cool as intended. CARB lists inverter thermal management among the components that hybrid OBD must monitor. Hyundai documents the code for the 2011 Sonata Hybrid (bulletin 14-HC-001), assigning it, like P0C73, to the electric water pump; symptoms include a hybrid warning, no EV mode and poor acceleration. Toyota recalled 2004–2009 Prius models (12V-536) because the inverter water pump could fail and cause a stall; that notice does not name a code. A leaking or air-locked circuit should also be checked.

causes.label: Electric inverter coolant pump failed or seized
Low coolant or air in the inverter circuit
Pump wiring, fuse or relay fault
Radiator fan not running or radiator blocked

symptoms: Hybrid system warning and MIL
No EV mode, reduced power
Vehicle may not start or may stall

P0A94.title: DC/DC Converter A Performance
P0A94.description: P0A94 reports that a DC/DC converter in the high-voltage system does not perform as commanded. In Toyota hybrids this is the boost converter inside the inverter assembly, which raises the battery voltage before it reaches the motor inverters. Toyota documents P0A94 for 2010–2015 Prius and 2012–2017 Prius v together with P0A1A, P324E and P3004 (bulletin T-SB-0003-21): the cause is damage in the inverter with converter, and the repair depends on the detail code. Recalls 14V-053 and 18V-684 address transistors in the intelligent power module that could overheat; the car then enters a fail-safe mode with reduced power. Not to be confused with the 14 V power module codes P0A86 to P0A8F.

causes.label: Damaged power transistors in the boost converter / inverter assembly
Thermal stress from insufficient inverter cooling
Outstanding recall or software update not performed

symptoms: MIL, hybrid system and other warning lamps
Fail-safe mode with greatly reduced power
Vehicle may stop and not restart

P0A95.title: High Voltage Fuse A
P0A95.description: P0A95 means the battery management detects that a fuse in the high-voltage circuit has opened, usually by comparing the voltage before and after the fuse. Several makers document it: Jaguar for the I-PACE battery energy control module, where a shorted high-voltage auxiliary component blows fuses in the junction box and battery module; Porsche for the Taycan as the main high-voltage fuse with a vehicle that will not become ready to drive; Volvo, whose procedure compares the voltage after the fuses with pack voltage; and Audi, which found an intermittent false entry in hard cornering fixed by software. P0E2F and P0E30 cover fuses B and C. Mostly the car cannot be driven until the cause is found.

causes.label: Short circuit in a high-voltage auxiliary component (e.g. compressor, heater)
Fuse opened after overload or ageing
Faulty voltage measurement or software misdetection in the battery control module

symptoms: Vehicle not ready to drive, propulsion warning
MIL or yellow warning lamp
Climate compressor or heater inoperative

P0A96.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Control Circuit/Open
P0A96.description: Some packs use two cooling fans; P0A96 reports an open or general fault in the control circuit of the second one. Ford documents it code-exact: on 2005–12 Escape Hybrid and 2006–11 Mariner Hybrid the traction battery control module may store P0A96, often together with P0A81 for fan 1, and the repair is to replace both high-voltage battery fans with a kit (about 3 hours, pack removal included). Ford notes the code alone usually causes no noticeable symptom. CARB requires the electronic outputs used for battery thermal management to be monitored. Short-circuit faults on fan 2 are P0A99 and P0A9A. If one fan fails, cooling capacity drops and power may be limited in heat.

causes.label: Fan 2 motor or electronics failed (Ford replaces both fans)
Loose connector or broken wire to fan 2
Blown fan fuse

symptoms: Code found during other diagnosis, often no complaint
Check engine or hybrid warning
Reduced hybrid power in hot conditions

P0A97.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Performance/Stuck Off
P0A97.description: P0A97 is the fan 2 counterpart of P0A82: the second battery cooling fan is electrically reachable but does not reach its requested speed or does not turn at all. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. CARB requires a functional check of battery cooling where feasible, and the methods are published for fan 1: GM compares commanded and measured speed (its sense code P0BC8), Toyota judges the deviation of the feedback-corrected duty, Honda compares expected and actual battery temperature rise. Blocked air paths and worn motors are the usual causes. Circuit faults on fan 2 are P0A96, P0A99 and P0A9A; the stuck-on case is P0A98. With one fan weak the pack runs warmer.

causes.label: Dust or debris on fan 2 or in its duct
Worn or seized fan 2 bearings
Blocked air intake to the battery
Faulty speed feedback from fan 2

symptoms: Hybrid warning or check engine light
Weak airflow from the battery vents
Reduced electric assist in warm weather

P0A98.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Stuck On
P0A98.description: P0A98 reports that battery cooling fan 2 keeps running after the controller has commanded it off; it mirrors P0A83 for fan 1. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. CARB calls for fan outputs to be checked for correct response to commands. GM's published method for fan 1 (sense code P0BC8) flags a fan that still reports more than about 250 rpm after being off for over 20 s; the same logic applies to a second fan. Typical causes are a welded relay, a control wire shorted to supply or fan electronics that ignore the stop command. Cooling is not at risk, but the fan can drain the 12 V battery and is audible after shutdown. Fan 2 circuit codes are P0A96, P0A99 and P0A9A.

causes.label: Welded fan 2 relay
Fan 2 control wire shorted to supply
Fan 2 internal controller ignores off command

symptoms: Battery fan audible after the vehicle is switched off
12 V battery discharged after parking
Hybrid or check engine warning

P0A99.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Control Circuit Low
P0A99.description: P0A99 reports a short to ground on the control circuit of the second battery cooling fan. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; Ford's two-fan Escape/Mariner Hybrid packs show that a second fan exists (there with P0A96). CARB requires the outputs used for battery thermal management to be monitored for circuit faults. The fan 1 counterpart P0A84 shows the usual GM logic: with the fan commanded at low duty, an output voltage below about 0.26 V in 16 of 20 samples sets a Type B code. The same approach is to be expected for fan 2. With the output held low the fan may not respond, cooling capacity falls and power may be limited. Open and high faults are P0A96 and P0A9A.

causes.label: Fan 2 control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in fan 2 control input
Moisture or corrosion in the fan 2 connector

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning
Fan 2 does not run when commanded
Reduced hybrid power in hot conditions

P0A9A.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Control Circuit High
P0A9A.description: P0A9A reports a short to voltage on the control circuit of the second battery cooling fan. No manufacturer publishes this exact code; CARB requires the electronic outputs of battery thermal management to be checked for circuit faults. The fan 1 counterpart P0A85 shows the usual method: GM samples the output while the fan is commanded between 11 % and 100 % duty and counts a voltage above 9 V as a failure, setting a Type B code after 16 of 20 samples. A fan 2 diagnosis would work the same way. Depending on the circuit design the fan runs constantly or stops responding; a constantly running fan can drain the 12 V battery. Open and low faults are P0A96 and P0A99; a mechanically stuck-on fan is P0A98.

causes.label: Fan 2 control wire shorted to supply voltage
Fan 2 control input internally open or shorted to supply
Corroded connector with leakage to supply

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning
Fan 2 runs constantly or not at all
Possible 12 V battery drain when parked

P0A9B.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0A9B.description: Temperature sensor A is one of the thermistors the battery controller uses to track cell or module temperature for cooling, charge limits and power limits. P0A9B is the general circuit code for this sensor: the controller finds an electrical fault it does not classify further as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for example, reports the sibling codes P0A9C to P0A9F instead. In those tables a failed sensor input is excluded from protection logic, and GM's Volt bulletin notes several sensors per pack. Expect a hybrid warning and reduced charge and assist power while the controller works with fewer valid temperatures. Check the sensor harness at the module sensing board before condemning the pack.

causes.label: Open, corroded or loose sensor wiring or connector inside the pack
Failed thermistor on the module or cell sensing board
Battery controller input or software fault

symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning and check engine light
Reduced electric assist, regeneration or charging power
Battery cooling fan or pump runs more than usual

P0A9C.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0A9C.description: This is a plausibility check: the reading of temperature sensor A is compared with the other sensors in the same pack, which should agree within a few degrees. GM sets P0A9C (Type B, two trips) when sensor A deviates from the average of the others by more than 25 °C for 50 of 67 samples (19OBDG02); Two-Mode hybrids use more than 15 °C against each other sensor for 90 of 100 samples, other programs more than 20 °C. The check is suspended while circuit low/high codes are active, so P0A9C points to a sensor that reads wrongly but stays in range. GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists it as sensor 1 performance and cures false sets with new module software. The pack then limits power to protect the cells.

causes.label: Thermistor drifted or poorly seated on its cell or module
High-resistance connection in the sensor circuit shifting the reading
Battery controller calibration causing false sets (GM Volt update)
Genuine local temperature difference from a cooling or cell problem

symptoms: Check engine light after two drive cycles
Reduced hybrid assist or charging power
Message such as battery too cold, plug in to warm (GM Volt)

P0A9D.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0A9D.description: Sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed through a pull-up resistor, so the voltage falls as the temperature rises; a short to ground looks like an absurdly hot cell. GM sets P0A9D (Type B, two trips) when the converted value exceeds 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples (19OBDG02); Two-Mode hybrids use above 95 °C while the other sensors read below 70 °C, other programs above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s. GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 names it sensor 1 circuit low voltage. The low-voltage case is the counterpart of P0A9E (open circuit, reads very cold) and differs from P0A7E, which reports a real overtemperature. Because the controller must assume heat, it cuts charge and discharge power and may run cooling at full speed.

causes.label: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground or chafed inside the pack
Internally shorted thermistor on the sensing board
Moisture or coolant in the sensor connector
Battery controller software causing false sets (GM Volt)

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Strongly reduced electric power or no EV mode
Battery cooling running at high speed without reason

P0A9E.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0A9E.description: With the NTC thermistor of sensor A on a pull-up circuit, an open sensor or wire drives the input voltage toward the reference, which the controller reads as an extremely cold cell. GM sets P0A9E (Type B, two trips) when the value falls below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples (19OBDG02); Two-Mode hybrids flag readings below -45 °C, other programs below -40 °C for 1.4 s. GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists it as sensor 1 circuit high voltage and pairs it with a battery too cold message at mild ambient temperatures. Unlike P0A9D the fault suggests an open circuit rather than a short. Because cold cells accept little current, the car restricts charging, regeneration and electric drive.

causes.label: Open sensor wire or unplugged connector inside the pack
Open (failed) thermistor on the sensing board
Signal shorted to the reference voltage
Battery controller software causing false sets (GM Volt)

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery too cold message although it is not cold
Little or no electric drive and weak regeneration

P0A9F.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0A9F.description: Cell temperature changes slowly, so a reading that jumps back and forth points to the circuit, not the battery. GM monitors this by summing the absolute sample-to-sample change of sensor A over a 10-sample window every 100 ms; if the sum exceeds 10, that window fails, and four failed windows out of five set P0A9F as Type B (two trips) in the 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables (16OBDG02, 19OBDG02). GM names a loose or intermittent connection as the typical trigger. The signal may still sit inside its valid range, which separates P0A9F from the hard low/high codes P0A9D/P0A9E and from the plausibility code P0A9C. The car protects the pack by limiting power and may show the fault only now and then.

causes.label: Loose, fretted or corroded pin in the sensor connector
Partly broken sensor wire that opens with vibration or heat
Electrical interference on the sensor line from high-voltage components

symptoms: Warning light that comes and goes
Temporarily reduced hybrid or EV power
Battery temperature value jumps in the scan tool data

P0AA0.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Circuit
P0AA0.description: The positive main contactor is a high-voltage relay that connects the positive pole of the traction battery to the propulsion bus. P0AA0 is the general fault code for this contactor circuit, used when the controller sees a problem it does not split into stuck closed (P0AA1), stuck open (P0AA2) or the control-circuit codes P0AD9 to P0ADC. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, Audi, Jeep and Mitsubishi report the specific siblings instead. NHTSA's Mach-E recall query shows the underlying failure modes: overheated contacts that stay open or weld shut. With the positive side unusable the car may refuse ready mode or drop propulsion; work on it requires high-voltage qualification.

causes.label: Positive contactor or battery junction box worn or damaged
Fault in the contactor coil feed or its connector
Weak 12 V supply so the contactor does not pull in reliably

symptoms: Vehicle does not enter ready or propulsion-active mode
Hybrid or EV system warning with check engine light
Possible loss of propulsion while driving

P0AA1.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Circuit Stuck Closed
P0AA1.description: P0AA1 means the positive main contactor conducts although it should be open, typically because its contacts have welded. GM checks this with all contactors commanded open for over 120 s (or the bus already below 9 % of pack voltage): more than 30 V on the positive bus in 4 of 6 samples sets Type B (two trips, 19OBDG02). Older GM programs test during precharge instead and set Type A after one trip if bus voltage exceeds 80 % (2011) or 60 % (2016) of pack voltage. GM bulletins cover the 2017 Bolt EV and welded contactors on the 2019 Volt; Jeep fixes false sets on the 2023 Grand Cherokee 4xe with software, Mitsubishi lists it as main contactor (+) seizure on the i-MiEV. The car may refuse to start.

causes.label: Positive contactor contacts welded, e.g. after high current or arcing
Battery or hybrid controller software (GM Volt 2019, Jeep 4xe updates)
Faulty battery disconnect unit (GM Bolt EV bulletin)
Bus voltage sensing error making an open contactor look closed

symptoms: Vehicle will not switch into ready or propulsion-active mode
Check engine light and service high voltage system message
Often stored together with P0AA4 or a slow discharge code such as P0C76

P0AA2.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Circuit Stuck Open
P0AA2.description: P0AA2 means the positive main contactor does not close, or does not conduct, when the controller commands it closed, so the high-voltage bus cannot be energised from the pack. Audi documents it for the 2020-2022 Q5 e quattro and 2021-2022 A7 e quattro plug-in hybrids: the car does not start and the battery management module stores P0AA2 (often with P0AA5). Audi traces rare cases to oxidised contact surfaces in the battery junction box after long standing or high humidity, and first prescribes repeated ignition cycles and an EV road test before replacing the junction box. GM lists the code among high-voltage faults for which Ultium EV pack data must be collected. Unlike P0AA1, the contacts are open, not welded.

causes.label: Oxidised contact surfaces after long standing or high humidity (Audi)
Failed battery junction box or burnt contactor
Contactor coil not energised due to wiring or 12 V supply fault

symptoms: Vehicle does not start or reach ready mode
Service high voltage battery or hybrid warning message
Possible sudden loss of propulsion if the contactor opens while driving

P0AA3.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Circuit
P0AA3.description: The negative main contactor switches the negative pole of the traction battery onto the propulsion bus; together with the positive contactor it isolates the pack completely when the car is off. P0AA3 is the general code for this contactor circuit when the fault is not reported more precisely as stuck closed (P0AA4), stuck open (P0AA5) or a control-circuit fault (P0ADD to P0AE0). No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, Audi, Jeep and Mitsubishi publish the specific siblings. Contact damage from heat and arcing, as described in NHTSA's Mach-E recall query, is the usual background. Expect a hybrid or EV warning and possibly no ready mode; diagnosis belongs to a high-voltage trained workshop.

causes.label: Negative contactor or battery junction box worn or damaged
Fault in the contactor coil wiring or connector
Battery controller driver or software fault

symptoms: Vehicle does not enter ready mode
Hybrid or EV system warning with check engine light
Charging may be refused

P0AA4.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Circuit Stuck Closed
P0AA4.description: P0AA4 reports that the negative main contactor still conducts while it should be open, usually through welded contacts, so the pack is no longer fully isolated on the negative side. GM tests it once all contactors have been commanded open for more than 120 s, or the bus has already decayed below 9 % of pack voltage: over 30 V on the negative bus in 4 of 6 samples at 12.5 ms sets Type B (two trips, 19OBDG02). GM's 2017 Bolt EV bulletin prescribes contactor cycling and then a new battery disconnect unit; the 2019 Volt update links welded contactors to P0AA1, P0AA4 and P0C76. Jeep cures false sets on the 2023 Grand Cherokee 4xe by software, and Mitsubishi calls it main contactor (-) seizure on the i-MiEV.

causes.label: Negative contactor contacts welded after high current or arcing
Battery or hybrid controller software (GM Volt 2019, Jeep 4xe updates)
Faulty battery disconnect unit (GM Bolt EV bulletin)
Negative bus voltage sensing error

symptoms: Vehicle will not start or switch into ready mode
Check engine light and high voltage system message
Often stored together with P0AA1 or the slow discharge code P0C76

P0AA5.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Circuit Stuck Open
P0AA5.description: P0AA5 is set when the negative main contactor stays open or fails to conduct after the controller has commanded it closed, so the negative side of the high-voltage bus never connects. Audi reports it, alone or with P0AA2, on the 2020-2022 Q5 e quattro and 2021-2022 A7 e quattro plug-in hybrids with a no-start complaint; the stated cause is oxidation of the contact surfaces in the battery junction box after very long standing or extreme humidity. Audi's procedure: several ignition cycles and an EV road test with many consumers on, and a new junction box only if the fault returns. GM includes P0AA5 among the Ultium EV high-voltage codes that require pack data retrieval. It is the counterpart of P0AA4 (welded contacts).

causes.label: Oxidised contact surfaces after long standing or high humidity (Audi)
Failed battery junction box or burnt negative contactor
Contactor coil not energised due to wiring or 12 V supply fault

symptoms: Vehicle does not start or reach ready mode
Hybrid or high voltage battery warning
Charging not possible

P0AA6.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage System Isolation Fault
P0AA6.description: The high-voltage system floats free of the chassis, and an isolation monitor measures the resistance from each HV rail to body ground. P0AA6 sets when that resistance falls below a calibrated limit. GM tables measure with the contactors open and fail below 75,000 ohms (2016) or 213,000 ohms (2019), Type A, one trip; Volt bulletins expect over 275 kOhm after repair, while FMVSS 305 sets 100 ohms per volt DC as the post-crash floor. Documented causes: Volt battery coolant leaks, a chafed HV harness on Ford Aviator/Explorer hybrids, a traction motor coolant leak on the 2017 Ioniq Hybrid; Toyota adds INF codes naming the area. P0AA7 to P0AAB flag the measuring circuit itself. Expect warnings, no charging or a stop-safely message.

causes.label: Coolant or moisture inside the battery pack, inverter or drive motor
Chafed or crushed orange HV cable shorting to the body
Insulation breakdown in the electric A/C compressor or a motor winding
Electrolyte leakage or contamination inside the battery sections

symptoms: Check engine and hybrid or EV system warning lights
Vehicle will not charge or will not enter ready mode after restart
Stop safely now message or reduced power

P0AA7.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Isolation Sensor Circuit
P0AA7.description: To measure isolation, the battery controller reads the voltage of each HV rail against chassis ground through an isolation sensor circuit and can switch in a known bias resistor. P0AA7 means this measuring circuit itself does not work, so the controller can no longer judge isolation. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables use it for a bias switch self-test: with all contactors open for 8 seconds after shutdown, switching the bias resistor must change both sensor readings; a combined change below 5 V squared sets the code, Type B, two trips. Mitsubishi lists P0AA7 to P0AA9 as leak detection circuit faults; on 2018 Outlander PHEVs noise caused false setting and a 60 km/h limit until restart, fixed by a sub-BMU update. P0AA6 is the actual insulation fault.

causes.label: Failed isolation bias switch or measuring circuit inside the battery controller
Controller software misreading electrical noise (update available on some models)
Open or loose isolation sense lead or connector at the battery

symptoms: Check engine and EV system service warnings
Power reduced or speed limited until the system is switched off and on
Regenerative braking warning on some models

P0AA8.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Isolation Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0AA8.description: The two isolation sensor readings, positive rail to ground and negative rail to ground, should together equal the total pack voltage. P0AA8 is the plausibility check of that relation. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables fail it when the sum of both readings differs from the measured battery voltage by more than 5 V in 40 of 50 samples, with the bias switch open, Type B, two trips. GM's 2013 table compares mid-pack sensors with the motor controller's voltage reading and allows 15 V. Mitsubishi groups P0AA8 with P0AA7 and P0AA9 as leak detection circuit faults, which on 2018 Outlander PHEVs were set falsely by noise. Unlike P0AA9 or P0AAA, the signal stays in range but is implausible; P0AA6 is a real insulation loss.

causes.label: Isolation measuring amplifier or reference in the battery controller out of tolerance
Pack voltage sense lead fault making the comparison value wrong
Controller software misreading electrical noise (update available on some models)

symptoms: Check engine and hybrid or EV system warnings
Reduced power or speed limit until restart
Isolation monitoring unavailable, so related faults may go unreported

P0AA9.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Isolation Sensor Circuit Low
P0AA9.description: P0AA9 reports that the isolation sensor signal sits below its valid window, typically because the sense line or the measuring input is pulled toward ground or has lost its supply. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables flag it when the sensor reads under 5 V with the bias switch open in 320 of 400 samples (about 5 s), Type B, two trips; the 2013 GM table uses a negative mid-pack reading under 5 V with contactors closed. Mitsubishi includes P0AA9 in its 2018 Outlander PHEV sub-BMU campaign together with P0AA7 and P0AA8, where noise caused false setting. The high counterpart is P0AAA. A low reading is a measuring fault, not proof of an insulation leak; that is P0AA6. Expect warnings and possibly reduced power.

causes.label: Isolation sense line shorted to ground or open input
Failed isolation measuring circuit in the battery controller
Controller software misreading electrical noise (update available on some models)

symptoms: Check engine and EV system warning lights
Reduced power or speed limit on some models

P0AAA.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Isolation Sensor Circuit High
P0AAA.description: P0AAA is the high-side counterpart of P0AA9: the isolation sensor reports a rail-to-ground voltage above anything the pack can produce. GM's tables tie the limit to the pack: over 333 V in the 2016 table and over 416 V in the 2019 table, each in 320 of 400 samples with the bias switch open, Type B, two trips. The 2013 GM table instead flags a mid-pack reading that differs from the motor controller's voltage by more than 15 V. Likely sources are an open reference or ground in the measuring circuit or a failed input stage in the battery controller. No public bulletin from another maker names this code. The car usually stays drivable with warnings, but isolation monitoring is lost, and P0AA6 cannot be trusted until it is fixed.

causes.label: Open ground or reference in the isolation measuring circuit
Failed isolation input stage in the battery controller
Sense lead shorted to another HV potential inside the pack

symptoms: Check engine and hybrid or EV warning lights
Isolation monitoring disabled while the code is active

P0AAB.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Isolation Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AAB.description: P0AAB covers an isolation sensor signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying wrong. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's hybrid tables use only P0AA7 to P0AAA for the measuring circuit. CARB requires hybrid input components to be monitored for circuit and rationality faults, which is the basis for this code. The best public analogue is Mitsubishi's 2018 Outlander PHEV campaign, where noise from the shift selector, brakes or A/C made the sub-BMU misjudge its leak detection circuit, setting P0AA7 to P0AA9. Check for software updates, then for loose connectors at the battery controller. Erratic readings can mask a true insulation fault (P0AA6). Expect warnings that come and go.

causes.label: Electrical noise misinterpreted by controller software
Loose or corroded sense connector at the battery controller
Failing isolation measuring circuit inside the controller

symptoms: Hybrid or EV warning lights that come and go
Occasional power limitation that clears after restart

P0AAC.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0AAC.description: Air-cooled hybrid batteries carry a thermistor in the cooling air path; GM calls sensor A the inlet air sensor. The battery controller uses it to run the fan and to judge cooling. P0AAC is the general circuit code, set for an electrical fault that is not classified as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports the siblings P0AAD to P0AAF instead, with Type B, two-trip logic. CARB requires hybrid component temperature sensors to be monitored like other input components. If the controller has no valid air temperature, it typically falls back to fixed fan control and may restrict battery power. Check connector and wiring at the air inlet duct first, then the sensor.

causes.label: Loose, corroded or damaged sensor connector or wiring at the air duct
Failed air temperature thermistor
Battery controller input or reference voltage fault

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid system warning light
Battery cooling fan runs constantly or at fixed speed
Reduced electric assist in hot conditions

P0AAD.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0AAD.description: P0AAD is the plausibility check for battery air temperature sensor A: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit other temperatures. GM documents two methods. In the 2011 and 2013 full-size two-mode hybrid tables, at power-up the inlet air reading may not exceed the outlet air reading by more than 20 °C, checked once per start. In GM's 2013 table (13OBDG05C), after more than 8 hours off the inlet sensor may not differ from the average battery core temperature by more than 10 °C, 50 of 62 samples. Both are Type B, two trips. A sensor stuck at a plausible value, a sensor out of the air stream or a faulty core sensor can cause it. The car keeps running, but fan control and power limits may be wrong.

causes.label: Thermistor drifted or stuck at a plausible value
Sensor displaced from the air stream or duct blocked
Fault in the comparison sensor (outlet air or cell temperature)

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery cooling fan behaves unusually

P0AAE.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0AAE.description: The battery air temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor, so a low signal voltage reads as very hot air. P0AAE sets when the signal stays below the lower limit, usually a short to ground. GM's 2013 table (13OBDG05C) uses under 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 samples; the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 flag an inlet reading above 95 °C in 30 of 40 samples. Both are Type B, two trips. Since the controller then assumes overheated cooling air, it may run the fan hard and cut battery power although nothing is hot. Look for chafed sensor wires touching ground or a sensor shorted internally. The opposite case, an open circuit reading as very cold, is P0AAF.

causes.label: Sensor signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Thermistor shorted internally
Battery controller input fault

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery cooling fan runs at high speed without reason
Reduced electric assist and regeneration

P0AAF.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0AAF.description: Air temperature sensor A is the thermistor GM places at the cooling air inlet of air-cooled hybrid packs. Being an NTC type, a high signal voltage means the controller sees implausibly cold air, typically from an open wire or a lost ground. GM's 2013 table 13OBDG05C sets P0AAF above 4.63 V, equal to about -45 °C, in 7 of 10 samples; the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 use a reading below -45 °C in 30 of 40 samples. All are Type B, two trips. The controller then ignores the inlet value, so fan control and the inlet-to-outlet comparison lose their reference. Check the connector at the inlet duct for a pushed-out pin first. The shorted counterpart reading as very hot is P0AAE.

causes.label: Open signal or ground wire between sensor and battery controller
Connector at the air inlet duct loose or with pushed-back pin
Thermistor open internally
Battery controller input fault

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Scan tool shows inlet air near -40 °C regardless of weather
Battery fan runs on a fixed default speed

P0AB0.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AB0.description: P0AB0 flags a battery air temperature sensor A signal that jumps faster than real air temperature can change, usually a sign of a loose contact rather than a dead sensor. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's two-mode and 2013 tables for sensor A only list the low, high and plausibility codes. GM does describe the method for the analogous cell sensor code P0A9F: the controller adds up the absolute signal changes over a 10-sample window and fails it when the sum exceeds a limit, 4 of 5 windows, Type B. CARB requires hybrid temperature inputs to be checked for such faults. Wiggle-test harness and connector at the inlet duct while watching live data before replacing the sensor.

causes.label: Loose or corroded contact at the inlet air sensor connector
Wire chafed through at the duct, intermittently touching ground
Electrical interference on the sensor line

symptoms: Hybrid warning light that comes and goes
Inlet air reading jumps in live data
Battery fan speed changes without obvious reason

P0AB1.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0AB1.description: Air temperature sensor B is a second thermistor in the battery cooling air path; in GM's two-mode hybrid tables it is the outlet air sensor behind the modules. P0AB1 is the general circuit code for it, used when the controller sees an electrical fault without sorting it into low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports the siblings P0AB2 to P0AB4 instead. CARB requires temperature inputs of hybrid components to be monitored for circuit faults. Without a valid outlet value the controller cannot judge how much heat the air carries away, so it usually falls back to a default fan strategy and may limit battery power. Inspect the outlet-side connector and wiring first.

causes.label: Damaged wiring or poor contact at the outlet air sensor
Air temperature sensor B failed
Battery controller input circuit fault

symptoms: Hybrid or check engine warning light
Battery fan runs on a default setting
Possibly reduced electric assist

P0AB2.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0AB2.description: P0AB2 checks whether air temperature sensor B reads sensibly. GM uses it on the full-size two-mode hybrids, where sensor B measures outlet air: in the 2011 and 2013 tables, with the battery fan commanded on, the outlet air may not be more than 10 °C warmer than the hottest battery module, 90 of 100 samples, Type B, two trips. The logic is simple physics: air leaving the pack cannot be much hotter than the modules that heated it. The test is skipped while module sensor or fan faults are present. A drifting thermistor, a sensor that has slipped out of the air stream or a faulty module sensor can trigger it. Unlike P0AB3 and P0AB4, the circuit itself is electrically in range.

causes.label: Outlet air thermistor drifted from its characteristic
Sensor displaced from its position in the air duct
Battery module temperature sensor used for comparison reads wrong
Corroded contact adding resistance

symptoms: Hybrid or check engine warning light
Outlet air reads clearly above module temperatures in live data
Usually no change in driving behavior

P0AB3.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0AB3.description: P0AB3 means the signal of air temperature sensor B sits below its valid range. Because the sensor is an NTC thermistor, a low voltage translates into very hot air, so a short to ground is the usual cause. GM documents the code for the outlet air sensor of its full-size two-mode hybrids: in the 2011 and 2013 tables it fails when the outlet reading exceeds 95 °C in 30 of 40 samples while at least one module sensor still reads below 70 °C, Type B, two trips. That extra condition separates a real overheat from a wiring fault. The controller may then run the fan at full speed and cut battery power without need. The open-circuit counterpart is P0AB4.

causes.label: Sensor B signal wire shorted to ground
Thermistor shorted internally
Moisture or debris bridging the connector pins

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery fan runs loud even when the pack is cool
Reduced electric assist and regeneration

P0AB4.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0AB4.description: P0AB4 reports a signal from air temperature sensor B above the valid range. For an NTC thermistor that reads as extremely cold air, which points to an open circuit, a broken ground or a disconnected plug. GM uses the code for the outlet air sensor of its full-size two-mode hybrids; the 2011 and 2013 tables set it when the outlet reading falls below -45 °C in 30 of 40 samples, Type B, two trips. With the outlet value rejected, the controller also suspends the outlet plausibility test P0AB2 and runs the fan on a substitute strategy. Look for a connector left off after battery work or a broken wire at the duct. The shorted counterpart is P0AB3, the inlet-side equivalent P0AAF.

causes.label: Open signal or ground wire of sensor B
Connector not refitted after battery or duct work
Thermistor open internally

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Outlet air shows about -40 °C in live data
Battery fan on default operation

P0AB5.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AB5.description: P0AB5 is set when the signal of battery air temperature sensor B fluctuates in a way real air temperature cannot, typically from an intermittent contact. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's two-mode tables, which use sensor B as the outlet air sensor, list only P0AB2 to P0AB4. As an analogy, GM's 2019 table judges the battery cell sensor code P0A9F by summing signal changes within 10-sample windows, failing after 4 of 5 bad windows, Type B. CARB requires hybrid temperature inputs to be checked for erratic behaviour. The fault often comes and goes with vibration or temperature. Move the outlet-side harness while watching live data to locate the weak point.

causes.label: Loose or corroded terminal at sensor B
Partly broken wire near the outlet duct
Interference coupled into the sensor line

symptoms: Hybrid warning light that appears intermittently
Outlet air value jumps in live data
No noticeable driving change in most cases

P0AB6.title: Engine Mount B Control Circuit/Open
P0AB6.description: Some engines sit on switchable or actively driven hydraulic mounts whose solenoid or actuator is energised by the engine controller. P0AB6 reports that the driver output for the second mount (B) sees an open or otherwise faulty circuit. Ford lists the code in its 2020-23 gasoline OBD summary under active mounts, assigns mount B to bank 2, monitors continuously and lets the low-level driver fault mature for about 5 seconds before storing it. On the 2008 Honda Pilot the same code covers the rear mount actuator. Mount A has the matching codes P0A14 to P0A16. Drivers mostly notice more vibration at idle or in cylinder-deactivation mode; the engine itself keeps running normally.

causes.label: Broken or chafed control wire to the mount actuator
Corroded or loose connector at the mount (splash zone)
Mount solenoid or actuator coil open internally
Output driver in the engine controller defective

symptoms: Check engine light on
Noticeable vibration at idle or with cylinder deactivation active
Cylinder deactivation may be suspended on some models

P0AB7.title: Engine Mount B Control Circuit Low
P0AB7.description: P0AB7 means the engine controller sees the control line of active engine mount B pulled too low, the usual signature of a short to ground or an actuator coil with too little resistance. Ford's 2020-23 gasoline OBD summary lists it among the active-mount checks for bank 2: the output driver flags the fault continuously and the PCM matures it within roughly 5 seconds. Honda describes the code on the 2008 Pilot as a low-current fault in the rear mount actuator circuit. P0AB6 covers the open circuit, P0AB8 the high side, and P0A15 the same fault on mount A. The driver usually feels more engine shake at idle; drivability is otherwise unaffected.

causes.label: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Mount solenoid coil shorted internally
Water ingress in the mount connector

symptoms: Check engine light on
Increased vibration felt through seat and steering wheel at idle

P0AB8.title: Engine Mount B Control Circuit High
P0AB8.description: With P0AB8 the controller finds the control circuit of active engine mount B at too high a level, for example because the line has a short to battery voltage or the driver cannot pull it down. Ford names the code in its 2020-23 gasoline OBD summary as the bank 2 high fault of the active-mount circuit check, which runs continuously and needs about 5 seconds of driver-reported fault before a code is stored. Honda's 2008 Pilot uses the B codes for the rear mount actuator. The open circuit is P0AB6, the low side P0AB7, and the mirror code for mount A is P0A16. Consequences are comfort-related: the mount stays in its default state and vibration rises at idle.

causes.label: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Mount actuator defective
Output driver in the engine controller defective

symptoms: Check engine light on
Rougher feel at idle and when pulling away

P0AB9.title: Hybrid/EV System Performance
P0AB9.description: Despite the broad title, GM uses P0AB9 for one concrete check: a failed engine auto-start or auto-stop in its hybrids, including an engine stall during that process. In the 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the hybrid controller sets the code when the engine still reports no torque about 15 seconds into an auto-start although more than 20 Nm is commanded, provided fuel level is sufficient and no cam or crank fault is present. The 2011 and 2013 tables describe the same idea with a stall during start/stop. GM rates it Type A, so the MIL comes on after one trip. Other faults that prevent starting, such as P0A0F, point at more specific causes; P0AB9 itself is the symptom.

causes.label: Fuel delivery problem (weak pump, nearly empty tank, clogged filter)
Ignition or injector fault that prevents the engine from firing
Starter-generator or motor unable to spin the engine to start speed
Controller software needing an update

symptoms: Check engine light on
Engine hesitates, fails or stalls when restarting at a stop
Auto-stop disabled for the rest of the trip

P0ABA.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense A Circuit
P0ABA.description: The battery management system measures the total voltage of the high-voltage pack through a dedicated sense circuit and uses it for state of charge, power limits and contactor checks. P0ABA is the general circuit fault for sense circuit A, set when the reading is unusable without being clearly low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for instance, monitors the same circuit with the more specific P0ABB to P0ABD. CARB requires hybrid battery inputs that feed emission-relevant control to be checked for circuit faults. Expect a warning light and reduced hybrid assistance, because the controller then works with conservative limits.

causes.label: Damaged or loose voltage sense lead inside the battery pack
Measurement input of the battery controller defective
Blown sense fuse or failed divider resistor

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid system warning light
Reduced electric assist or EV range
Vehicle may not enter ready mode

P0ABB.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense A Circuit Range/Performance
P0ABB.description: P0ABB is a plausibility check: the measured pack voltage is within electrical limits but does not agree with what the individual cells add up to. GM documents it in several hybrid tables. From 2016 the battery controller flags it when pack voltage and the sum of cell voltages differ by more than 10 V in 32 of 40 samples; the 2013 table compares the pack reading with 32 times the average cell voltage and uses a 5.49 V limit. Both are Type B, so the MIL needs two trips. The check is suppressed while cell voltage circuit faults are active. P0ABC and P0ABD cover hard low or high readings, P0AF8 compares the pack sensor with the inverter bus voltage.

causes.label: Pack voltage measurement drifted (divider or input aging)
Faulty cell voltage tap distorting the cell sum
High-resistance busbar or sense connection

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid system warning light
Erratic state-of-charge display
Reduced electric power

P0ABC.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense A Circuit Low
P0ABC.description: P0ABC is stored when the pack voltage sensor reports a value below anything the battery could really have, pointing to a short to ground or a lost sense signal rather than a discharged pack. GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables set it below 4.8 V with system voltage above 10.2 V, after 8 failed samples out of 10 taken every 25 ms, and rate it Type A with MIL on the first trip. The 2013 table for an earlier hybrid uses a limit of 30 V, 7 of 10 samples and Type B. A real deep discharge is handled by other codes such as P0AFA. Because the controller no longer trusts pack voltage, hybrid operation is restricted or the vehicle will not go ready.

causes.label: Sense line shorted to ground or disconnected
Sense fuse or link open so no voltage reaches the input
Battery controller measurement input defective

symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Vehicle may refuse to enter ready mode
Engine runs continuously, no electric drive

P0ABD.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense A Circuit High
P0ABD.description: The counterpart to P0ABC: the pack voltage reading is above the highest value the battery could physically reach, which suggests an open reference, a failed divider or a damaged input rather than real overcharging. GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables set P0ABD above 392 V, again with 8 failed samples out of 10 at 25 ms intervals and Type A, so the MIL comes on immediately. For the smaller pack in its 2013 table the limit is 190.1 V, with 7 of 10 samples and Type B. Range and plausibility problems are reported by P0ABB, the low limit by P0ABC. The vehicle typically limits or blocks electric operation until the fault is cleared.

causes.label: Open ground or reference side of the sense circuit
Voltage divider component failed in the battery controller
Battery controller measurement input defective

symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Electric drive limited or unavailable

P0ABE.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0ABE.description: P0ABE flags a pack voltage signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of changing smoothly, as a battery voltage physically would. A loose sense connection or a cracked solder joint inside the pack are the classic triggers. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM covers the same sensor with P0ABB, P0ABC and P0ABD, and its battery controller cross-checks the pack reading against the cell sum and the inverter bus voltage (P0AF8). CARB demands circuit and rationality monitoring for such battery inputs. Because the faults come and go, the code may be stored without lasting symptoms, but power limits and warning lights can appear during the dropouts.

causes.label: Loose or fretted voltage sense connection
Cracked solder or crimp joint on the sense board
Electrical noise from damaged shielding or ground

symptoms: Warning light that comes and goes
Sudden short drops in electric power

P0ABF.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A Circuit
P0ABF.description: The pack current sensor, usually a Hall-effect unit around the main cable, tells the battery controller how much current flows in and out. P0ABF is the general fault of sensor A. GM uses it in its 2019 hybrid controller tables as a stuck-in-range check: before the high-voltage bus is precharged the controller stores a zero-current baseline, then expects a measurable change once precharge starts or the main contactor closes and loads such as the inverter and auxiliary power module draw current. If the reading moves by less than 1 A, P0ABF fails. Out-of-range readings are P0AC1 and P0AC2, offset errors P0AC0. Without a valid current value state of charge cannot be tracked, so power is limited.

causes.label: Hall current sensor output frozen
Sensor supply, ground or signal wire faulty
Sensor not seated around the conductor after repair

symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Reduced electric power and erratic charge display
Vehicle may not go ready

P0AC0.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0AC0.description: P0AC0 belongs to the battery current sensor family, not to battery cooling. It reports a sensor whose reading is electrically valid but implausible. GM's 2011 to 2013 hybrid tables describe the check: with the contactors open, when no current can flow, the reading in each of the sensor's high, mid and low ranges must stay within 5 A of zero, and the controller also checks that the measured current fits the change in pack voltage. A failure sets the code as one-trip Type A in the 2013 table. The check waits while circuit codes P0AC1 or P0AC2 are active. Effects are a drifting charge estimate, reduced hybrid power and, in severe cases, a vehicle that will not go ready.

causes.label: Current sensor zero offset drifted
Unstable sensor supply or reference voltage
Battery controller input fault

symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
State of charge display drifts or jumps
Reduced electric assist

P0AC1.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A Circuit Low
P0AC1.description: P0AC1 is set when the output of the pack current sensor falls below the valid window, so that the converted current would be an impossible discharge or charge value. GM documents it in several hybrid tables. In the 2016 and 2019 versions the Hall-effect sensor fails when the result is below -365.1 A for 8 of 10 samples at 25 ms with system voltage above 10.2 V; the code is Type A with MIL on the first trip. An earlier GM pack in the 2013 table uses an output below 0.2 V, equal to about -230 A, with 7 of 10 samples and Type B. Typical causes are a lost supply or a signal shorted to ground. P0AC2 is the high side and P0AC0 the plausibility check.

causes.label: Sensor 5 V supply open or shorted
Signal wire shorted to ground
Hall current sensor failed internally

symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Electric drive limited or vehicle will not go ready

P0AC2.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A Circuit High
P0AC2.description: With P0AC2 the current sensor output sits above its valid window, which after conversion would mean an implausibly large current in the opposite direction to P0AC1. GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables set it when the Hall-effect sensor reads above 274.6 A in 8 of 10 samples taken every 25 ms, again as Type A with immediate MIL. The 2013 table for an earlier pack uses an output above 4.65 V, roughly 215 A, with 7 of 10 samples and Type B. A signal shorted to the 5 V supply or an open sensor ground are common reasons. Because the controller can no longer count charge, it caps battery power; the low limit is P0AC1 and implausible offsets are P0AC0.

causes.label: Sensor ground open
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V supply or another voltage
Hall current sensor failed internally

symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Battery power limited, engine runs more often

P0AC3.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AC3.description: P0AC3 describes a battery current signal that jumps, spikes or drops out in a way real current flow could not explain, typically through a loose connector, a chafed signal wire or interference on the sensor ground. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM monitors the same Hall-effect sensor with the stuck check P0ABF, the offset check P0AC0 and the range limits P0AC1 and P0AC2, and CARB requires circuit and rationality monitoring for battery inputs that influence emissions. As the fault is not permanent, the code may be the only trace; during the dropouts the controller may still cut battery power or turn on a warning light.

causes.label: Loose or corroded current sensor connector
Chafed signal or supply wire with intermittent contact
Interference on sensor ground or shield

symptoms: Warning light that comes and goes
Short drops in electric power while driving

P0AC4.title: Hybrid/EV Powertrain Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P0AC4.description: In many hybrids the hybrid powertrain controller has its own emission-related diagnostics but does not drive the malfunction indicator lamp itself. When it detects such a fault it sends a MIL request to the engine controller, which then stores P0AC4 as a pointer. GM documents this in its 2011, 2013, 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables: the engine controller watches the request message continuously once 3 seconds have passed after power-up and logs P0AC4 after one trip, listed as Type A but marked No MIL because the lamp is owed to the original fault. The real cause is therefore stored in the hybrid controller and must be read there. P0A7B is the equivalent request from the battery energy control module.

causes.label: Emission-related fault stored in the hybrid controller
Request still present because codes were cleared only in the engine controller

symptoms: Check engine light on (caused by the underlying hybrid fault)
Further codes present only in the hybrid controller

P0AC5.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0AC5.description: Battery temperature sensor B is one of several thermistors that measure cell or module temperature inside the high-voltage pack; GM's Volt bulletin calls it sensor 2 of nine. P0AC5 is the general circuit code for it, used for an electrical fault the controller does not classify as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for instance, reports P0AC6 to P0AC9 instead. CARB requires hybrid battery temperature inputs to be monitored for circuit faults. With one sensor missing the controller has a gap in its temperature picture and tends to limit charge and discharge power. The sensor usually sits on a module or sensing board inside the pack, so checks need high-voltage safety procedures.

causes.label: Poor contact or damaged wire between sensor B and sensing board
Temperature sensor B failed
Fault in the battery controller input stage

symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning
Reduced electric power and regeneration
Charging may be slower on plug-in models

P0AC6.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0AC6.description: P0AC6 is the plausibility test for battery temperature sensor B: its reading is compared with the other pack sensors. GM documents several calibrations. The 2016 and 2019 tables fail it when the sensor differs from the average of the other sensors by more than 25 °C, 50 of 67 samples; the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 use more than 15 °C, 90 of 100 samples; GM's 2013 table 13OBDG05C allows 8.55 °C after more than 6 hours off. All are Type B, two trips. Bulletin 18-NA-342 for the Chevrolet Volt lists P0AC6 among false sensor codes in cold weather and fixes them by reprogramming. Otherwise a drifting sensor or a real local hot spot in a module is likely.

causes.label: Controller software flags the sensor falsely (GM Volt bulletin 18-NA-342)
Sensor B drifted from its characteristic
Corroded contact adding resistance in the sensor circuit
Real temperature difference from a weak cell or blocked cooling

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
One sensor reading far off the others in live data
Battery too cold message on the Volt in mild weather

P0AC7.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0AC7.description: P0AC7 means the voltage of battery temperature sensor B is below its valid range. GM's sensors are NTC thermistors, so a low voltage equals an extremely hot reading, usually from a short to ground. The thresholds differ by program: the 2016 and 2019 tables fail it above 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples; the two-mode tables of 2011 and 2013 above 95 °C in 30 of 40 samples; GM's 2013 table 13OBDG05C below 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10. All are Type B, two trips. GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 names P0AC7 among sensor codes that can set falsely and calls for a software update. A genuine hot pack would trip far lower thresholds first, so treat P0AC7 as an electrical fault.

causes.label: Sensor B signal shorted to ground inside the pack harness
Thermistor shorted internally
Controller software setting the code falsely (Volt bulletin 18-NA-342)
Moisture or coolant at the sensing board connector

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Sensor B shows an implausibly high temperature
Charging and drive power reduced

P0AC8.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0AC8.description: P0AC8 reports that battery temperature sensor B delivers a voltage above its valid range, which for an NTC thermistor reads as extreme cold. An open wire, a disconnected sensing board plug or a broken sensor are typical. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables set it below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples, the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 below -45 °C in 30 of 40, and GM's 2013 table 13OBDG05C above 4.63 V, about -45 °C, in 7 of 10; all Type B, two trips. In the Chevrolet Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342 links such codes to a Battery Too Cold message above -25 °C ambient and prescribes reprogramming. A pack believed to be frozen gets strict charge and power limits.

causes.label: Open signal or return wire of sensor B
Thermistor open internally
Controller software issue on the Volt (bulletin 18-NA-342)
Signal shorted to the reference voltage

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery too cold message although it is not cold
Strongly reduced charging and electric power

P0AC9.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AC9.description: P0AC9 catches a battery temperature sensor B signal that changes erratically. Pack temperatures move slowly because of the large thermal mass, so rapid swings point to a bad connection. GM documents the method in its 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables: the controller integrates the absolute change of the sensor value over a 10-sample window at 100 ms per sample; a window fails when the sum exceeds 10, and the code sets after 4 of 5 failed windows, Type B, two trips. The older two-mode and 2013 tables have no erratic code for this sensor. The fault is often intermittent and may clear by itself, so check connector locking and terminal tension at the sensing board.

causes.label: Loose terminal or unlatched connector at the sensing board
Partly broken sensor wire inside the pack
Interference from high-voltage switching on the sensor line

symptoms: Hybrid warning light that comes and goes
Sensor B value jumps in live data
Occasional power limitation

P0ACA.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P0ACA.description: Battery temperature sensor C is a further thermistor inside the high-voltage pack, corresponding to sensor 3 in GM's Volt bulletin. P0ACA covers a general electrical fault in its circuit that the controller does not narrow down to low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports the more specific siblings P0ACB to P0ACE instead. CARB requires temperature sensors of hybrid batteries to be monitored like other input components. Losing one temperature input makes the controller more cautious: expect reduced charge and assist power and a hybrid warning. Since sensors C and B often share the same sensing board, check whether neighbouring sensor codes are stored as well.

causes.label: Poor contact or damaged wire between sensor C and sensing board
Temperature sensor C failed
Fault in the battery controller input stage

symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning
Reduced electric power and regeneration
Further battery sensor codes may be stored

P0ACB.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0ACB.description: With P0ACB the controller judges battery temperature sensor C implausible: its value deviates too far from what the other pack sensors report. GM applies the same limits as for sensors A and B. In the 2016 and 2019 tables the threshold is more than 25 °C away from the average of the other sensors in 50 of 67 samples; the 2011 and 2013 two-mode tables use more than 15 °C in 90 of 100; the 2013 table 13OBDG05C uses 8.55 °C after a soak of more than 6 hours. All are Type B, two trips. The Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 includes P0ACB among codes corrected by software. Without a bulletin, compare all sensors after an overnight soak to see whether only sensor C stands out.

causes.label: Sensor C drifted from its characteristic
Controller software flags the sensor falsely (GM Volt bulletin 18-NA-342)
Corroded terminal adding resistance
Real temperature difference in the module monitored by sensor C

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Sensor C reads clearly off the others after a long soak
Possibly reduced charge and drive power

P0ACC.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P0ACC.description: P0ACC sets when the signal of battery temperature sensor C drops below the valid voltage window. For the NTC sensors GM uses, that equals an impossibly hot reading, most often caused by a short to ground in the pack wiring. GM's thresholds for sensor C mirror those for B: above 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples in the 2016 and 2019 tables, above 95 °C in 30 of 40 in the two-mode tables of 2011 and 2013, and below 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 in the 2013 table 13OBDG05C; always Type B, two trips. Bulletin 18-NA-342 lists P0ACC for the Chevrolet Volt and prescribes a software update first. After that, inspect the sensor C wiring and the sensing board for chafing or moisture.

causes.label: Sensor C signal shorted to ground
Thermistor shorted internally
Controller software setting the code falsely (Volt bulletin 18-NA-342)
Moisture at the sensing board connector

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Sensor C shows an implausibly high temperature
Reduced charging and electric drive power

P0ACD.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P0ACD.description: P0ACD indicates that battery temperature sensor C reports a voltage above its plausible range, which an NTC sensor translates into extreme cold. Common reasons are an open circuit, a pin backed out of the sensing board connector or a cracked thermistor. GM sets the code below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples in its 2016 and 2019 tables, below -45 °C in 30 of 40 on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode hybrids, and above 4.63 V, about -45 °C, in 7 of 10 in the 2013 table 13OBDG05C; Type B, two trips. On the Chevrolet Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342 ties it to a false Battery Too Cold message and a reprogramming fix. A seemingly frozen pack is heavily limited in charge and discharge.

causes.label: Open signal or return wire of sensor C
Thermistor open or cracked
Controller software issue on the Volt (bulletin 18-NA-342)

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery too cold message in mild weather
Strongly reduced charging and electric power

P0ACE.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0ACE.description: P0ACE flags erratic behaviour of battery temperature sensor C, meaning the reading jumps faster than the heavy battery mass could ever warm or cool. In GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the controller sums the absolute changes of the sensor value across a 10-sample window taken every 100 ms; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 store the code as Type B, two trips. This is the same logic GM uses for sensors A and B. The older two-mode and 2013 programs do not list an erratic code for sensor C. Typical culprits are a loose terminal, a partly broken wire or a connector not fully latched after pack service. Several jumping sensors at once point to the sensing board.

causes.label: Loose terminal or unlatched connector at sensor C
Partly broken sensor wire inside the pack
Fault on the battery sensing board affecting several inputs

symptoms: Hybrid warning light that appears intermittently
Sensor C value jumps in live data
Occasional power limitation

P0ACF.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 3 Control Circuit/Open
P0ACF.description: Air-cooled traction batteries can use several blowers; P0ACF belongs to the third one and means the battery controller sees an open or otherwise invalid control line while it drives fan 3. CARB 1968.2 (e)(15.2.3)(B) requires the electrical inputs and outputs of the battery thermal management to be monitored like other comprehensive components. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; GM shows the method on fan 1 (P0A81): it checks the control voltage on the driver output and needs 16 failures before a Type B code is stored. Fan 1 and fan 2 have their own sets P0A81 and P0A96. Without the third blower the pack heats up faster, and power is limited.

causes.label: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at fan 3
Broken control wire between battery controller and fan 3
Fan motor or its built-in driver open internally
Fan output stage in the battery controller defective

symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning light, often with check engine light
Electric drive power reduced when the battery gets warm
No fan noise from the battery area when cooling is expected

P0AD0.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 3 Performance/Stuck Off
P0AD0.description: P0AD0 is a functional fault: the control line of battery fan 3 may be electrically fine, but the blower does not deliver what was commanded, or stays still. Depending on design, the controller compares fan speed feedback with the request, or, as a Honda patent describes, compares the expected battery temperature change for the known cooling capacity with the measured one. CARB asks for such a functional check of the battery cooling where feasible. No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD0 itself; circuit faults of the same fan are P0ACF, P0AD2 and P0AD3, the opposite case is P0AD1. The driver usually sees a hybrid warning and reduced power on hot days.

causes.label: Fan intake or duct blocked by dirt, pet hair or objects (often under or beside a seat)
Worn bearings or debris slowing the fan wheel
Speed feedback signal from fan 3 missing or implausible
Weak 12 V supply or poor ground at the fan

symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning light
Power or regeneration limited after longer drives or in heat
Battery temperature rises faster than usual

P0AD1.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 3 Stuck On
P0AD1.description: P0AD1 is the counterpart to P0AD0: fan 3 of the traction battery keeps turning although the controller has switched it off or commanded a lower level. A speed feedback or the current in the fan circuit shows that the blower still runs. CARB 1968.2 requires the battery thermal management outputs to be checked for proper response to commands. No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD1; for fan 1 GM treats an unwanted speed above about 250 rpm with the fan off under its own code P0BC8. Typical causes are a driver stage stuck on or a short to supply voltage. Effects are an audible fan after shutdown and possible 12 V battery drain rather than a drivability problem.

causes.label: Fan output stage in battery controller or fan module stuck on
Control wire chafed against a supply voltage
Fan relay contacts welded (relay-switched designs)

symptoms: Battery fan audible after the vehicle is switched off
12 V battery discharged after standing
Hybrid or EV warning light

P0AD2.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 3 Control Circuit Low
P0AD2.description: P0AD2 reports that the control signal for battery fan 3 is pulled too low, typically a short to ground on the line between battery controller and blower. Such fans are mostly speed-controlled by a PWM duty cycle, as a Toyota patent on battery fan control explains. No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD2; GM sets the analogous fan 1 code P0A84 when the control voltage stays below 0.257 V with system voltage above 9.1 V, Type B with two trips. The open circuit is P0ACF, a short to voltage P0AD3. CARB requires these electrical checks for battery thermal components. Fan 3 then cannot be driven, and the battery may run warm with limited power.

causes.label: Control wire chafed through to body ground
Internal short in fan 3 motor or its electronics
Moisture or spilled liquid in the fan connector
Output stage in the battery controller defective

symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning light, often with check engine light
Electric drive power reduced when the battery gets warm
No fan noise from the battery area when cooling is expected

P0AD3.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 3 Control Circuit High
P0AD3.description: With P0AD3 the battery controller finds the control line of cooling fan 3 at a voltage that is too high for the commanded state, pointing to a short to a supply voltage or a fan input that no longer pulls the line down. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; GM's analogous fan 1 code P0A85 trips when the control voltage exceeds 9 V while the fan is driven, Type B. Siblings: P0AD2 for the low side, P0ACF for an open line, P0AD1 if the fan keeps running. CARB 1968.2 calls for this circuit monitoring on battery thermal management parts. Depending on the fault the fan runs permanently or not at all, and the pack may be derated.

causes.label: Control wire shorted to 12 V or another supply
Fan electronics no longer loading the control line
Bent or bridged pins in the fan connector
Battery controller output stage defective

symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning light
Fan 3 runs constantly or not at all
Reduced electric power when the battery is warm

P0AD4.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Flow System Insufficient Air Flow
P0AD4.description: P0AD4 is a system-level check of air-cooled traction batteries: the controller concludes that too little air passes the cells, for example because the cell temperatures rise faster than the commanded fan level allows, as a Honda fan diagnosis patent describes. CARB 1968.2 asks for a functional check of the battery cooling performance where feasible. Stellantis lists P0AD4 for the 48 V eTorque battery of the Ram 1500 (TSBs 08-033/034/035-24, 2022-24) and cures some cases with a battery pack control module software update. Unlike the fan circuit codes, P0AD4 is often caused by a blocked intake or duct. Expect a warning lamp and limited assist or electric power.

causes.label: Cabin air intake grille or duct of the battery blocked (bags, clothing, dust, pet hair)
Battery air filter clogged, where fitted
Battery fan running too slowly
Battery controller software sets the code falsely (Ram eTorque, fixed by update)

symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Reduced electric assist or start-stop not available
Battery fan runs loud for long periods

P0AD5.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Flow Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P0AD5.description: Some air-cooled battery packs route their cooling air through a motorized flap that switches between cabin air, recirculation or an outlet. P0AD5 means the battery controller finds the drive circuit of this valve A open or otherwise faulty. No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD5; the same component appears in Audi's Q5 hybrid (2012-15) bulletin, where the battery management module J841 works with the learned end stops of the air supply valve in the cooling module. CARB 1968.2 requires electrical monitoring of all battery thermal management outputs. Sibling codes are P0AD6 (range/performance), P0AD7 (low) and P0AD8 (high). The flap stays where it is, and the controller may cut electric operation.

causes.label: Loose or corroded connector at the flap actuator
Broken wire in the actuator harness
Actuator motor winding open
Output stage in battery controller defective

symptoms: Hybrid warning, electric drive may be switched off
Check engine light on
Battery temperature not controlled as usual

P0AD6.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Flow Valve A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0AD6.description: P0AD6 flags that the air flow valve A of the battery cooling does not behave as expected: the circuit is intact, but position, travel or the learned end stops do not fit the command. Audi documents exactly this code as P0AD600 on the 2012-15 Q5 hybrid (TSB 2038152): a software error made the battery management module J841 lose the learned end stops of the air supply valve, electric and hybrid drive were disabled, and a software update to version 0543 fixed it. CARB 1968.2 calls for functional monitoring of battery thermal management. Pure circuit faults are P0AD5, P0AD7 and P0AD8. Besides software, a sticking flap or a slipping actuator can cause it.

causes.label: Battery controller software loses learned end stops (Audi Q5 hybrid, fixed by update)
Flap binding from dirt or a deformed duct
Actuator gears or position feedback worn
End stops not relearned after battery or actuator work

symptoms: Hybrid drive system error message in the cluster
Electric and hybrid operation no longer available
Check engine light on

P0AD7.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Flow Valve A Control Circuit Low
P0AD7.description: P0AD7 sets when the control circuit of the battery air flow valve A reads too low a voltage, usually a short to ground in the line or actuator. The valve is a motorized flap in the battery cooling duct, as in the Audi Q5 hybrid cooling module, whose bulletin covers the range/performance sibling P0AD6. No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD7 itself, so thresholds and debounce times are unknown. CARB 1968.2 requires battery thermal management outputs to be checked for circuit faults. Neighbours are P0AD5 (open) and P0AD8 (high). With the flap no longer movable, cooling may be impaired and the hybrid system may restrict electric operation.

causes.label: Actuator control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the flap actuator
Moisture in the actuator connector
Battery controller output stage defective

symptoms: Hybrid warning, electric drive may be switched off
Check engine light on
Battery temperature not controlled as usual

P0AD8.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Flow Valve A Control Circuit High
P0AD8.description: With P0AD8 the battery controller sees too high a voltage in the drive circuit of air flow valve A, typically a short to a supply voltage or an actuator that no longer draws current. The component is the motorized flap that directs cooling air through an air-cooled traction battery, documented for example in Audi's Q5 hybrid bulletin on the related code P0AD6.
