No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD8; exact limits are not published. CARB 1968.2 requires circuit monitoring of battery thermal management outputs. Compare P0AD7 for the low side and P0AD5 for an open circuit. The flap may stay in one position, so cooling and electric drive can be restricted.

causes.label: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Actuator no longer loading the circuit
Bridged or bent pins in the connector
Battery controller output stage defective

symptoms: Hybrid warning, electric drive may be switched off
Check engine light on
Battery temperature not controlled as usual

P0AD9.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Control Circuit/Open
P0AD9.description: The positive main contactor connects the traction battery to the high-voltage bus; its coil is driven by the battery or hybrid controller. P0AD9 covers an open in this coil circuit. GM documents it in detail: in hybrid tables from model year 2011 the HPC2 sets it on open load during the commanded state, Type B. 2016-19 tables use a control voltage between 1.15 and 2.81 V with the contactor commanded off, 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms; 2019 versions also check coil current below 194 mA when on. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid outputs. Low and high faults are P0ADB and P0ADC; a contactor stuck open is P0AA2. The car usually cannot go ready.

causes.label: Open in the contactor coil or its pigtail inside the battery disconnect unit
Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the battery disconnect unit
Broken control wire in the battery harness
High-side driver in the battery controller defective

symptoms: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible

P0ADA.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0ADA.description: P0ADA describes a positive contactor coil circuit that is electrically present but does not behave plausibly: coil current, voltage or response time outside the expected window, for instance due to high resistance or an unstable PWM hold signal. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; GM, which details the positive contactor driver codes P0AD9, P0ADB and P0ADC with Type B logic and sample counters, does not list P0ADA. CARB 1968.2 requires functional and rationality checks of hybrid output components. It must be separated from the contact-side codes P0AA1 (stuck closed) and P0AA2 (stuck open). Drivers may see intermittent no-start or loss of ready mode.

causes.label: High resistance in coil wiring or connector (corrosion, fretting)
Contactor coil degraded or partially shorted
Low 12 V supply during contactor closing
Battery controller fault or software

symptoms: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible

P0ADB.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Control Circuit Low
P0ADB.description: P0ADB means the drive circuit of the positive main contactor reads too low, mostly a short to ground. GM uses it widely: 2016-19 tables set it when the control voltage stays under 5.35 V with the contactor commanded on, 13 of 16 samples, Type B. The 2013 eAssist battery controller checks the low-side driver in the off state for a short to ground or an open circuit, 3 of 5 samples, two trips. Audi lists P0ADB00 in battery management 2 (J1120) of 2019-22 A6 to Q8 models with a software fix (TSB 2066205), and Dodge names it for the 2024 Charger EV (TSB 08-071-25). The battery then cannot be connected, so the vehicle will not become ready.

causes.label: Coil control wire shorted to ground
Contactor coil internally shorted
Battery controller software sets the code (Audi, Dodge bulletins)
Driver stage in the battery controller defective

symptoms: Vehicle does not start; multiple warnings in the cluster
Hybrid or EV warning light
Charging not possible

P0ADC.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Control Circuit High
P0ADC.description: P0ADC indicates that the positive contactor drive circuit carries too much voltage for the commanded state, usually a short to battery voltage. In GM's 2016-19 hybrid tables the driver output, with the contactor commanded off, reads between 5.27 and 19.7 V for 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B with two trips. The 2013 eAssist controller sets it for a short to power on the low-side driver in the on state, 3 of 5 samples. CARB requires such circuit monitoring for hybrid components. Siblings are P0AD9 (open) and P0ADB (low). A short to power can energize the coil unintentionally, so the contactor may not open when it should.

causes.label: Coil control wire shorted to 12 V
Damaged harness or connector at the battery disconnect unit
Driver stage in the battery controller shorted

symptoms: Hybrid or EV warning light
High-voltage system disabled, vehicle not ready
Possible related stuck-closed codes

P0ADD.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit/Open
P0ADD.description: The negative main contactor closes the return path of the traction battery; P0ADD reports an open in its coil drive circuit. GM documents the code in parallel to the positive side: tables since model year 2011 detect open load in the HPC2 and store it after two trips; 2016-19 tables evaluate a control voltage between 1.15 and 2.81 V while off, 40 of 50 samples, Type B, and 2019 tables add a coil current check below 194 mA when on. CARB 1968.2 covers this circuit monitoring of hybrid components. Related codes are P0ADF and P0AE0 for low and high, P0AA5 for a contactor stuck open, P0AD9 for the positive side. Without this contactor the HV system stays off.

causes.label: Open in negative contactor coil or its pigtail
Loose or corroded connector at the battery disconnect unit
Broken control wire in the battery harness
Driver in the battery controller defective

symptoms: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible

P0ADE.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0ADE.description: P0ADE is set when the coil circuit of the negative main contactor works electrically but its values are implausible, such as coil current or hold voltage out of range or a slow response after the command. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; GM, whose tables cover the negative contactor driver codes P0ADD, P0ADF and P0AE0 in detail, does not use P0ADE. CARB 1968.2 requires rationality and functional checks on hybrid output components. The contact-side faults P0AA4 (stuck closed) and P0AA5 (stuck open) are separate diagnoses. Possible effects are an intermittent failure to reach ready mode or charge.

causes.label: High resistance in coil wiring or connector
Negative contactor coil degraded
Weak 12 V battery during start-up
Battery controller fault or software

symptoms: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible

P0ADF.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit Low
P0ADF.description: P0ADF reports that the drive circuit of the negative main contactor is pulled too low, typically a short to ground in the coil line. GM documents the code in its 2016-19 hybrid tables: control voltage below 5.35 V while the contactor is commanded on, 13 of 16 samples at 12.5 ms (20 of 25 in one 2016 group), Type B with two trips, enabled above about 9 to 10 V on the 12 V system. CARB 1968.2 requires this kind of circuit monitoring for hybrid outputs. Counterparts are P0ADD (open), P0AE0 (high) and, on the positive side, P0ADB. As the contactor cannot close properly, the high-voltage system does not come up and the vehicle will not drive or charge.

causes.label: Coil control wire shorted to ground
Negative contactor coil internally shorted
Moisture in the battery disconnect unit connector
Driver in the battery controller defective

symptoms: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible

P0AE0.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit High
P0AE0.description: P0AE0 is stored when the negative contactor drive circuit shows too high a voltage for its state, which mostly means a short to battery voltage. GM's 2016-19 hybrid tables set it with the contactor commanded off and the driver output between 5.27 and 19.7 V for 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B, two trips. CARB 1968.2 requires hybrid output components to be monitored for such circuit faults. Siblings are P0ADD (open) and P0ADF (low); the positive side equivalent is P0ADC. A coil energized by a short could keep the contactor closed, so a stuck-closed code P0AA4 may follow. The controller usually disables the high-voltage system.

causes.label: Coil control wire shorted to 12 V
Damaged harness or connector at the battery disconnect unit
Driver stage in the battery controller shorted

symptoms: Hybrid or EV warning light
High-voltage system disabled, vehicle not ready
Possible additional stuck-closed code

P0AE1.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Circuit
P0AE1.description: Before the main contactors close, a precharge contactor routes battery current through a resistor so the inverter capacitors fill slowly instead of drawing a damaging inrush. P0AE1 is the general fault of this precharge path when it is not split into stuck closed (P0AE2), stuck open (P0AE3) or a driver fault (P0AE4 to P0AE7). Honda lists P0AE1 as a bypass contactor malfunction in bulletins 20-030 (2012-15 Civic Hybrid) and 20-021 (2013 ILX Hybrid); there a cracked solder joint in the motor power inverter is the cause and the whole inverter is replaced. Mercedes-Benz names P0AE173 on the G 580 with EQ technology after unplugging the AC charger too early. Expect no ready mode or no charging.

causes.label: Defective solder joint in the motor power inverter (Honda IMA)
Precharge contactor or precharge resistor failed
Fault logged by battery controller software after an interrupted charging sequence
Wiring or connector fault in the contactor circuit

symptoms: Hybrid or EV system warning in the cluster
Vehicle does not become ready to drive
Charging not possible

P0AE2.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Closed
P0AE2.description: P0AE2 means the precharge path conducts although it should be open, for example welded contacts or a precharge switch that no longer turns off. GM's 2011 Volt table checks it once per precharge event: if the bus voltage already exceeds 80 % of pack voltage before precharge begins, the precharge FET is judged stuck closed, 4 of 4 samples, Type A with MIL after one trip. Mitsubishi lists P0AE2 as charging contactor seizure on the 2012 i-MiEV (TSB-12-54-014). Audi names it for the 2022 e-tron GT with a software fix, and Dodge and Jeep list P0AE2-00 for the 2025 Charger EV and 2024 Wagoneer S, where a battery pack replacement may be required. The car may refuse to start.

causes.label: Precharge contactor contacts welded or precharge switch shorted
Battery controller software sets the code falsely (Audi, Stellantis bulletins)
Contactor driver held on by a short to power
Bus voltage not discharged before the next precharge

symptoms: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Wrench symbol or service message in the cluster

P0AE3.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Open
P0AE3.description: P0AE3 is set when the precharge path does not conduct after it has been commanded closed, so the bus voltage fails to rise and the main contactors are not allowed to close. GM documents several cases: preliminary information PIC6165A for the 2016-17 Chevrolet Volt describes a rare P0AE3 in cool weather right after a completed charge, without driveability effects; parts should not be replaced, a new calibration followed, and the MIL goes out after three clean drive cycles. GM bulletin 23-NA-151 lists P0AE3 among high-priority codes on Ultium EVs that call for battery stability checks. Audi includes P0AE300 for the 2022 e-tron GT. Unlike P0AE2, the contacts stay open; a slow precharge is P0C78.

causes.label: Battery controller calibration sets the code under certain conditions (GM Volt, Audi)
Precharge contactor contacts burnt or coil not pulling in
Precharge resistor or its fuse open
Internal fault in the battery disconnect unit

symptoms: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL or service engine soon light on
No battery charge level shown after switching on

P0AE4.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor A Control Circuit/Open
P0AE4.description: P0AE4 concerns the circuit that drives the coil of precharge contactor A, not its contacts. GM uses it in many hybrid and EV tables, with changing logic: the 2016 and 2019 OBDG02 tables look for an open high-side driver circuit, a control voltage between 1.15 and 2.81 V while commanded off, 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B, two trips. The 2019 OBDG01 version also catches a short to power while off and a coil current below 194 mA while on. The 2011 Volt table instead flags a short to battery voltage in the off state, Type A, one trip. With the coil not driven, precharge cannot start and the high-voltage system stays off. Low and high variants are P0AE6 and P0AE7.

causes.label: Open control wire or loose connector at the contactor coil
Precharge contactor coil open internally
Control wire shorted to 12 V (GM 2011 and 2019 logic)
Driver stage in the battery or hybrid controller defective

symptoms: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Charging not possible

P0AE5.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0AE5.description: P0AE5 reports that the precharge function works electrically but does not deliver the expected result, so the controller judges the circuit implausible. Ford documents it in special service message SSM 47129: 2013-18 C-MAX and Fusion Hybrid and Energi models and the MKZ Hybrid may not start, with P0AE5 stored in the battery energy control module. When pinpoint tests show that the DC/DC converter, the cabin coolant heater or the A/C compressor has a low internal resistance on its high-voltage side, Ford replaces only that component, not the battery junction box. A load that drags the bus down keeps the precharge from reaching its target. Open, low and high driver faults are P0AE4, P0AE6 and P0AE7.

causes.label: High-voltage consumer with low internal resistance (DC/DC converter, coolant heater, A/C compressor)
Precharge resistor degraded or wrong value
Precharge contactor responding slowly or with high contact resistance

symptoms: Vehicle does not start or become ready
Red warning triangle or hybrid warning in the cluster
Possible additional codes from the faulty high-voltage consumer

P0AE6.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor A Control Circuit Low
P0AE6.description: P0AE6 means the control line of precharge contactor A is pulled too low, usually a short to ground. GM documents it in several programs. The 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables test the high-side driver while the contactor is commanded on and fail it below 5.35 V, 13 of 16 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B with two trips, enabled above 10.2 V system voltage. GM's 2013 eAssist battery controller uses a low-side driver and flags low voltage in the off state, which there points to a short to ground or an open circuit, 3 of 5 samples at 50 ms, Type B. CARB requires such circuit checks on hybrid outputs. Because the coil cannot pull in, precharge never starts; the positive main contactor equivalent is P0ADB.

causes.label: Control wire chafed and shorted to ground
Precharge contactor coil shorted internally
Open circuit on low-side driven designs (GM eAssist)
Driver stage in the battery controller defective

symptoms: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid warning on
Engine start or electric drive unavailable

P0AE7.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor A Control Circuit High
P0AE7.description: P0AE7 is stored when the control line of precharge contactor A carries too much voltage for its commanded state, typically a short to the 12 V supply. In GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the high-side driver output reads between 5.27 and 19.7 V while the contactor is commanded off, 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B, two trips. GM's 2013 eAssist controller looks for a short to power on its low-side driver in the on state, 3 of 5 samples at 50 ms, Type B. A coil energized by a short may keep the precharge path closed when it should be open, so P0AE2 can follow. CARB requires circuit monitoring of such hybrid outputs. The negative and positive main contactor counterparts are P0AE0 and P0ADC.

causes.label: Control wire shorted to 12 V supply
Driver stage stuck on in the battery controller
Outdated battery controller calibration

symptoms: Vehicle may not start or become ready
MIL and hybrid warning on
Possible additional stuck-closed code P0AE2

P0AE8.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit
P0AE8.description: Battery temperature sensor D is a further thermistor inside the high-voltage pack; GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists the matching codes as temperature sensor 4 of nine. P0AE8 is the general circuit code for it, used when the controller finds an electrical fault without classifying it as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables report the more specific siblings P0AE9 to P0AEC instead. CARB requires temperature inputs of hybrid batteries to be monitored for circuit faults. With one value missing, the controller has a gap in its temperature picture and usually limits charge and discharge power. The sensor sits on a module or sensing board inside the pack, so checks require high-voltage safety procedures.

causes.label: Poor contact or damaged wire between sensor D and sensing board
Temperature sensor D failed
Fault in the battery controller input stage

symptoms: Hybrid system or check engine warning
Reduced electric power and regeneration
Further battery sensor codes may be stored

P0AE9.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance
P0AE9.description: P0AE9 is the plausibility check for battery temperature sensor D, GM's sensor 4: its reading is compared with the other pack sensors. In GM's 2016 and 2019 tables it fails when the value is more than 25 °C away from the average of the others in 50 of 67 samples; the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 use more than 15 °C in 90 of 100; the eAssist table 13OBDG05C allows 8.55 °C after a long module off time; GM's 2018 table uses 20 °C for 5 s within 6.7 s. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 counts P0AE9 among sensor codes that set falsely in cold weather and fixes them by reprogramming. Otherwise a drifting sensor or a real hot spot in one module is the likely cause.

causes.label: Outdated controller software (GM Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342)
Temperature sensor D drifting out of tolerance
Genuine local temperature difference in one battery module
Increased contact resistance in the sensor circuit

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Battery Too Cold message despite mild weather (Volt)
Reduced charge and electric drive power

P0AEA.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low
P0AEA.description: P0AEA means the voltage of battery temperature sensor D is below its valid range. GM uses NTC thermistors with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a low voltage reads as an extremely hot cell, usually from a short to ground. Thresholds vary: above 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples in the 2016 and 2019 tables; above 95 °C in 30 of 40 on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode hybrids; below 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 in the eAssist table 13OBDG05C; above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s in a 2018 controller. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists P0AEA among codes that can set falsely and calls for a software update first. A genuinely hot pack would trip lower limits earlier, so treat it as electrical.

causes.label: Sensor D signal wire shorted to ground
Temperature sensor D internally shorted
Outdated controller software (GM Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342)
Moisture or damage on the battery sensing board

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Charge and drive power strongly limited
Battery cooling running more than usual

P0AEB.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit High
P0AEB.description: P0AEB reports that battery temperature sensor D delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensors this reads as extreme cold, pointing to an open wire, a backed-out pin at the sensing board or a cracked thermistor. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables set it below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples, the 2011 and 2013 two-mode hybrids below -45 °C in 30 of 40, the eAssist table 13OBDG05C above 4.63 V, about -45 °C, in 7 of 10, and a 2018 controller below -40 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s; all Type B, two trips. On the Chevrolet Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342 links such codes to a Battery Too Cold message above -25 °C ambient and prescribes reprogramming. A pack the controller believes frozen gets strict charge and power limits.

causes.label: Open circuit or unplugged connector at sensor D
Outdated controller software (GM Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342)
Temperature sensor D open internally

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Battery Too Cold message (Volt)
Charging and electric drive restricted

P0AEC.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AEC.description: P0AEC flags erratic behaviour of battery temperature sensor D: the reading jumps faster than the heavy battery mass could ever warm or cool. GM documents the method in its 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables. The controller sums the absolute changes of the sensor value across a 10-sample window taken every 100 ms; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 store the code as Type B, two trips. GM applies the same logic to sensors A to C. The older two-mode and eAssist tables list no erratic code for sensor D. Typical culprits are a loose terminal, a partly broken wire or a connector not fully latched after pack service. If several sensors jump at once, suspect the sensing board rather than the individual thermistor.

causes.label: Loose terminal or connector not fully latched at sensor D
Partly broken or chafed sensor wire
Fault on the battery sensing board

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips, may go out again
Jumping battery temperature in live data
Occasional power limitation

P0AED.title: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0AED.description: The inverter of an electric drive motor carries thermistors near its power switches so the controller can derate before the IGBTs overheat. In GM's hybrid tables, inverter temperature sensor A is the phase U sensor of the inverter for motor A. P0AED is the general circuit code for it, used for an electrical fault that is not classified as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports the specific siblings P0AEE, P0AEF and P0AF0 instead. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components and their sensors for circuit faults. Without a valid inverter temperature the controller has to assume the worst and usually limits motor torque. The sensor is built into the power inverter module, so repair often means replacing that unit.

causes.label: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor

symptoms: Hybrid system warning or check engine lamp
Reduced electric drive power
Possible loss of electric drive

P0AEE.title: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0AEE.description: P0AEE checks whether inverter temperature sensor A reads sensibly. GM's 2016 to 2019 tables compare it after a cold soak with an average temperature of the vehicle; more than 20 °C apart sets Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt compares it with the other power electronics sensors (20 °C, Type A), the 2013 two-mode trucks after 360 minutes off (15 °C), eAssist with module and MGU temperatures (20 °C). GM bulletin PIC6303A notes that on Volt, Malibu and LaCrosse with 5ET50 the code alone triggers no remedy; the inverter is only replaced with P0AC4. Audi fixes P0AEE00 on Q5 and A7 e quattro by software, and Honda lists it among inverter faults of the 2012-15 Civic Hybrid with extended warranty.

causes.label: Controller software error (Audi Q5/A7 e quattro bulletin)
Inverter temperature sensor A drifting out of tolerance
Failing power inverter module (e.g. Honda MPI solder joints)
Uneven inverter cooling after soak

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp, often without drivability change
Drive system fault warning (Audi)
Vehicle may not start in hybrid mode

P0AEF.title: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0AEF.description: P0AEF means the signal of inverter temperature sensor A is below its valid range. GM describes it as an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a low voltage reads as an impossibly hot inverter, usually a short to ground or an internal sensor fault. GM's thresholds: above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, in the 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables; above 159 °C, Type A, one trip, in another 2019 table; above 150 °C on eAssist; above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; above 125 °C, Type B, on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks. Stellantis lists P0AEF-11 for the 2026 Jeep Compass PHEV outside the US among codes behind an Electric Traction System Fault and a no-start, repaired by replacing the inverter.

causes.label: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Electric drive power cut back strongly
Vehicle may not start (Jeep Compass PHEV)

P0AF0.title: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0AF0.description: P0AF0 reports a signal from inverter temperature sensor A above its valid range, which for an NTC sensor reads as an extremely cold inverter: open wire, lost ground or a broken sensor. GM's 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables set it below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, but only after at least 90 s of inverter warm-up at 20 Nm or more, so a really cold car does not trigger it; Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt uses below -58 °C (Type A), eAssist below -70 °C and the two-mode trucks below -40 °C (Type B). Kia's 2025 Sorento Hybrid bulletin lists P0AF0 with P0A3C and P1B77 after intermittent motor operation during engine clutch learning and fixes it with a motor control unit update.

causes.label: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Motor control unit software (Kia Sorento Hybrid 2025)
Loose or corroded connector at the inverter

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Reduced electric drive power
Traction motor noise or inoperative A/C (Kia)

P0AF1.title: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AF1.description: P0AF1 is meant for an inverter temperature sensor A signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of failing permanently. Inverter heat sinks are liquid-cooled and change temperature smoothly, so sudden steps point to a contact problem or an internal fault in the sensing circuit. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables cover sensor A only with the plausibility, low and high codes P0AEE, P0AEF and P0AF0. GM's method for erratic battery sensors, such as P0AEC, sums signal changes over 10-sample windows and fails after 4 of 5 bad windows, which shows how such a check usually works. CARB requires hybrid sensor inputs to be monitored for this kind of fault. Freeze-frame data help, since the fault often comes and goes.

causes.label: Loose or corroded connector at the inverter module
Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module
Electrical interference on the sensor signal

symptoms: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief power reductions while driving
Jumping inverter temperature in live data

P0AF2.title: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0AF2.description: Inverter temperature sensor B is, in GM's hybrid tables, the phase U thermistor of the second inverter, the one that drives motor B in two-motor systems. P0AF2 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault that the controller does not narrow down to low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's tables report the specific siblings P0AF3, P0AF4 and P0AF5 instead. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components and their sensor circuits. Without a valid temperature the controller cannot protect the power switches of inverter B and usually limits that motor's torque. Whether a vehicle uses sensor B at all depends on its layout, so read the full code list and check the inverter connectors.

causes.label: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor

symptoms: Hybrid system warning or check engine lamp
Reduced electric drive or generator power
Higher fuel consumption in hybrid operation

P0AF3.title: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0AF3.description: P0AF3 is the plausibility test for inverter temperature sensor B, the phase U sensor of GM's motor B inverter. In the 2016 to 2019 tables the sensor is compared after a cold soak with a calculated average vehicle temperature; a difference above 20 °C sets the code, Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt compares it with the other power electronics sensors at 20 °C, Type A, and the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks after 360 minutes off at 15 °C, Type B. GM bulletin PIC6303A lists P0AF3 with P0AEE and the other inverter thermistor codes on 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal with the 5ET50 drive: alone they cause no noticeable effect, and the inverter is replaced only if P0AC4 set at the same time.

causes.label: Inverter temperature sensor B drifting out of tolerance
Failing power inverter module
Uneven inverter coolant flow after soak

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Often no noticeable drivability change
Further inverter temperature codes may be stored

P0AF4.title: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0AF4.description: P0AF4 reports a signal of inverter temperature sensor B below the valid range. GM uses an NTC thermistor with a pull-up, so a low voltage reads as an inverter far hotter than possible, usually from a short to ground or an internal sensor fault in the motor B inverter. GM's thresholds: above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips, in the 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables; above 159 °C, Type A, one trip, in another 2019 table; above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; above 125 °C, Type B, on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks. A genuine overheat is reported separately as an over-temperature code such as P0A3D or P0C14. Because the sensor sits inside the inverter, the fix is usually the inverter assembly.

causes.label: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Motor B power strongly limited
Reduced hybrid assist and regeneration

P0AF5.title: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0AF5.description: P0AF5 means inverter temperature sensor B delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensor that equals an implausibly cold inverter, so an open circuit, a lost ground or a cracked thermistor is likely. In GM's 2016 to 2019 tables the code sets below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, but only once the inverter has run at least 90 s at 20 Nm or more, which rules out a genuinely cold start; Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt uses below -58 °C with Type A, one trip; the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks use below -40 °C, Type B. Until the value is valid, the controller protects inverter B with substitute values and may reduce motor B power. Check connectors at the inverter before condemning the unit.

causes.label: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the inverter
Lost sensor ground

symptoms: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Reduced motor B power
Implausibly cold inverter temperature in live data

P0AF6.title: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AF6.description: P0AF6 targets an inverter temperature sensor B signal that jumps or drops out briefly. Since the heat sink of the motor B inverter is liquid-cooled and warms or cools gradually, abrupt changes in the reading indicate a contact problem or an intermittent fault in the sensing circuit rather than real temperature. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables only list P0AF3, P0AF4 and P0AF5 for sensor B. For erratic battery temperature sensors such as P0AEC, GM sums the signal changes over 10-sample windows and fails after 4 of 5 bad windows, a likely model for this check. CARB requires sensor inputs of hybrid systems to be checked for erratic behaviour. Watch live data while gently moving the inverter harness.

causes.label: Loose or corroded connector at the inverter module
Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module
Electrical interference on the sensor signal

symptoms: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief reductions of motor B power
Jumping inverter temperature in live data

P0AF7.title: 14 Volt Power Module Internal Temperature Too High
P0AF7.description: The 14 V power module is the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery in hybrids and EVs. P0AF7 reports that its internal temperature has exceeded the protection limit, a real overheat rather than a sensor circuit fault. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM's 2013 eAssist table shows how the same module is watched: its Accessory Power Module has two temperature sensors with their own circuit codes, and the separate code P0C32 compares sensor 1 with a thermal model and fails if they differ by more than 15 °C. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components. Common causes are a blocked cooling path, a weak coolant pump or fan, or a constantly high 12 V load. The module then derates its output, so the 12 V battery may run down.

causes.label: Restricted cooling, weak coolant pump or failed cooling fan
Sustained high 12 V load or weak 12 V battery
Internal fault of the DC/DC converter

symptoms: Warning lamp or 12 V charging warning
Low 12 V voltage, flickering lights
Comfort consumers switched off

P0AF8.title: Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage
P0AF8.description: P0AF8 compares the battery pack voltage reported by the battery controller with an independent measurement on the high-voltage bus. GM calls it system voltage correlation: with the contactors closed, the 2019 tables fail it when the pack reading differs from the inverter bus voltage by more than 13.95 V, or from the charger bus voltage by more than 14.95 V, 400 of 500 samples at 25 ms, Type A. The 2011 Volt table uses 12 V and Type A, the 2013 eAssist table 5.77 V against the motor controller, Type B. GM's Saturn Vue Hybrid PIP4005A links P0AF8 with P0AFB to a loose negative battery cable, and Volt PIC6089B mentions it with low 12 V system faults. P0AFA and P0AFB judge the voltage level itself.

causes.label: Loose or arcing high-voltage battery cable connection
Pack or bus voltage sensing circuit inaccurate
Low 12 V supply or loose 12 V power fuse affecting the measuring modules
High resistance in a pack fuse or main contactor

symptoms: MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Battery saver or low battery message
Intermittent no crank or reduced hybrid power

P0AF9.title: Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage Unstable
P0AF9.description: P0AF9 is meant for a traction battery voltage that fluctuates more than load changes can explain, for example through a loose terminal, an intermittent contactor or a cell group that collapses under load. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for instance, covers system voltage with P0AF8 (correlation), P0AFA and P0AFB (low and high), and reports uneven cell groups as P0BBE pack voltage variation, which bulletin 19-NA-117 ties to degraded cells in the Volt and ELR. CARB requires hybrid battery inputs to be monitored for circuit and rationality faults. Typical effects are intermittent power limits and warnings; check high-voltage connections and cell voltages under load.

causes.label: Loose high-voltage terminal or busbar connection
Degraded cell group collapsing under load
Main contactor with intermittent contact

symptoms: Intermittent hybrid or EV warning
Sudden power reductions while driving
Code may come and go without lasting symptoms

P0AFA.title: Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage Low
P0AFA.description: P0AFA protects the traction battery from deep discharge: the pack voltage, or in some versions any cell voltage, has fallen below a temperature-dependent limit. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables set it after 320 of 400 samples (about 10 s) for the pack or 112 of 140 for a cell, Type A, and latch it so that only a technician command can clear it. GM bulletins name causes: degraded cell groups in 2011-15 Volt and ELR (19-NA-117), a blown fuse in the Bolt EV manual disconnect lever (18-NA-225), cell contamination in the 2015 Spark EV (17-NA-131) and repeated cranking that empties the Malibu Hybrid pack (PIC6229). A Ram eTorque parts notice names it for the 48 V power pack. Expect a no-start.

causes.label: Degraded or self-discharging cell groups
Pack drained by repeated failed engine starts or long standing
Open high-voltage fuse or manual disconnect
Loose or high-resistance ground on 48 V systems

symptoms: Vehicle does not start; restart blocked while the code is latched
Reduced or lost propulsion before the no-start
Plug-in charging not possible

P0AFB.title: Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage High
P0AFB.description: P0AFB guards against overcharging: the pack voltage, or a single cell, exceeds a temperature-dependent upper limit. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables use 320 of 400 samples (about 10 s) for the pack and 112 of 140 for a cell, Type A, and latch the code until a technician clears it by command; the 2011 Volt table also uses Type A. On the 2007-09 Saturn Vue Hybrid, GM's PIP4005A finds P0AFB together with P0AF8 caused by a loose negative battery cable. Mercedes-Benz uses P0AFB00 on 48 V starter-alternator systems for an on-board voltage that is too high, with software fixes for M256 engines, S-Class and GLE/GLS. Toyota's Prius Prime tech tip uses P0AFB11 with a current sensor text.

causes.label: Loose or arcing battery cable causing voltage spikes
Control unit software allows overvoltage (Mercedes 48 V bulletins)
Cell imbalance so that one cell overcharges
Faulty voltage sensing reporting too high a value

symptoms: Hybrid system or MIL warning
Start-stop or regenerative braking disabled
Possible no crank on mild hybrids

P0AFC.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Sensor Module
P0AFC.description: Some hybrid packs carry a separate sensor module that measures block voltages and passes them to the battery controller; Toyota calls it the battery voltage sensor or battery smart unit. P0AFC reports a fault of this module itself, such as a failed self-check or disturbed data transfer. Toyota documents it for the 2012-2015 Camry Hybrid in tech tip T-TT-0359-15 (repair manual entry P0AFC-123): an aftermarket antenna in the trunk, for example for CB radio, can set the code, and relocating it is the first step before following the regular diagnosis. CARB requires hybrid battery inputs to be monitored. Without valid block voltages the hybrid system usually shuts down or limits power.

causes.label: Radio interference from an aftermarket antenna near the battery (Toyota Camry Hybrid)
Battery voltage sensor module internally defective
Supply or communication wiring of the sensor module faulty

symptoms: MIL and check hybrid system warning on
Hybrid drive disabled or reduced
Code may return when the radio transmitter is used

P0AFD.title: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Temperature Too Low
P0AFD.description: P0AFD indicates that the traction battery is colder than its permitted operating range. At very low temperatures cell resistance rises and charging risks lithium plating, so the controller restricts or blocks charging and discharging. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. As a related case, GM's bulletin 18-NA-342 describes a Chevrolet Volt showing Battery Too Cold, Plug in to Warm above -25 °C because of faulty temperature sensor readings, fixed by reprogramming. CARB requires hybrid battery temperature inputs and their plausibility to be monitored. Distinguish a genuinely cold pack, which warms up on the charger or through the battery heater, from a sensor or heater fault; sensor circuit faults have their own codes.

causes.label: Vehicle parked unplugged in extreme cold
Battery heater or coolant heater not working
Temperature sensor reading too cold (sensor or software)

symptoms: Battery too cold message in the cluster
Reduced electric power or electric drive unavailable
Charging slow or not possible until the pack warms up

P0AFE.title: Hybrid/EV Battery System Voltage Too Low for Voltage Step Up Conversion
P0AFE.description: Many hybrids raise the battery voltage with a step-up (boost) converter before it reaches the inverters; Toyota's second-generation Hybrid Synergy Drive, for example, boosts a pack of around 200 V to 500 V or more. The converter needs a minimum input voltage to reach its target without excessive current. P0AFE is set when the battery-side voltage is below that minimum, so the converter cannot boost properly. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; CARB requires hybrid components such as converters to be monitored for functional faults. A deeply discharged or weak pack, a high-resistance connection or a voltage measurement fault are the obvious suspects. Expect reduced electric assist; a low pack voltage is reported separately as P0AFA.

causes.label: Pack deeply discharged or weak under load
High-resistance connection between battery and converter
Converter input voltage measured too low

symptoms: Hybrid system warning
Reduced acceleration and electric assist
Engine runs more often than usual

P0AFF.title: System Voltage Too Low for Voltage Step Down Conversion
P0AFF.description: A step-down (buck) DC/DC converter, often called the accessory power module, supplies the 12 V system from the high-voltage or 48 V bus. To regulate its output it needs an input voltage above a minimum. P0AFF is set when the input system voltage is too low for this conversion, so the converter cannot hold its 12 V output. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM monitors the related function in its 2013 eAssist table: P0CA2 flags a step-down failure of the 14 V power module after a shoot-through fault in its switching device, one trip, Type A. CARB requires such hybrid components to be monitored. Expect a charging system warning and a slowly draining 12 V battery.

causes.label: High-voltage or 48 V bus voltage too low (discharged pack, open contactor)
High-resistance input connection or fuse of the DC/DC converter
DC/DC converter internal measuring fault

symptoms: Battery or charging system warning light
12 V battery discharges, electrical consumers fail
Hybrid or start-stop functions restricted
